title: Descriptive Phrases
subtitle: Several words doing one adjective's job.
objectives: Use adjective phrases to add detail
Place a descriptive phrase next to what it describes

cards.title: A phrase can do an adjective's job
cards.text: 'The red fan' uses one word. 'The fan with the cracked guard' uses four and tells you far more.

cards.title: A group of words describing a noun
cards.text: No verb of its own. It just hangs onto a noun and adds information.
points: **with the cracked guard** — describes which fan.
**in the blue corner** — describes which fighter.
**covered in dust** — describes its condition.
**Each one answers** which, what kind, or whose.

question.text: In 'the fan with the cracked guard', the descriptive phrase is…
question.explain: It tells you which fan, which is an adjective's job done by a phrase.

cards.title: Put it next to the thing it describes
cards.text: English decides what a phrase modifies by where you put it. Move it and the meaning moves.
points: **The fan in the corner was broken.** The fan is in the corner.
**In the corner, the fan was broken.** Same meaning, still fine.
**Move it too far** and it attaches to the wrong noun.
**Next to its noun** is the safe rule.

cards.title: Describing which part you mean
cards.text: On a bench with parts everywhere, a phrase is how you say exactly which one.
points: **The screw from the back plate.** Not any screw.
**The capacitor with the bulging top.** The faulty one.
**The blade nearest the motor.**
**Precision is the whole point** of a descriptive phrase.

cards.title: "I saw the fan walking to school"
cards.alt: A cartoon electric fan with human legs striding along a pavement
cards.text: Read literally, this is what the sentence says. The phrase grabbed the wrong noun.

cards.title: When the phrase grabs the wrong noun
cards.text: The sentence stays grammatical and becomes ridiculous, which is how you spot it.
points: **'I saw the fan walking to school.'** The fan was not walking.
**Fix:** *Walking to school, I saw the fan.*
**The phrase attaches** to whatever is closest.
**Read it literally.** If it is absurd, move the phrase.

question.text: 'Covered in dust, I found the old fan.' says the dust was on me.
question.explain: Read literally, the phrase attaches to 'I'. Move it next to 'fan' to fix it.

cards.title: A report has to say exactly which thing
cards.text: After a storm, 'the house was damaged' is useless. Which house?
points: **The house nearest the river** flooded first.
**The bridge on the coast road** is closed.
**Families living below the dam** were moved.
**The phrase is the information.**

options: Looking in the drawer, I found the manual.
I found looking in the drawer the manual.
I found the manual looking in the drawer.
The manual I found looking drawer.
question.explain: The phrase sits next to 'I', which is who was looking.

cards.title: What is the word pointing at?
cards.text: Make the call three times. A wrong pick shows you what it would mean.

cards.title: Literature Review: Don Quixote, Chapter 18: In Search of Dulcinea
cards.text: Quixote sets out to find a woman who exists mostly in his description of her.
points: **A lady of great beauty and noble birth** — his phrase.
**A farm girl from a nearby village** — everyone else's.
**Same person**, described two ways.
**The phrase makes the character**, which is the whole joke.

terms.def: A group of words describing a noun.
Anything that adds detail to another word.
A phrase sitting next to the wrong noun.
The person, place or thing being described.

cards.title: What to remember
points: A descriptive phrase does an adjective's job with several words.
It answers which, what kind, or whose.
Put it next to the noun it describes.
If the literal reading is absurd, the modifier is misplaced.

quiz.explain: It adds detail to a noun, like an adjective made of several words.

quiz.text: In 'the blade nearest the motor', the phrase is…
Where should a descriptive phrase go?
options: Next to the noun it describes
quiz.explain: Position decides what it attaches to.
quiz.objective: Place a descriptive phrase next to what it describes

quiz.text: 'I saw the fan walking to school.' The problem is…
quiz.explain: Read literally, the fan is walking.

options: The fan walking I saw to school.
I walking saw the fan to school.
Walking to school, I saw the fan.
I saw walking to school the fan.
quiz.explain: Now the phrase sits next to 'I'.

quiz.text: A descriptive phrase contains its own main verb.
quiz.explain: It has no verb of its own. It hangs onto a noun.

quiz.text: 'The house nearest the river' tells you…
quiz.explain: Which one — that is an adjective's job.
quiz.objective: Use adjective phrases to add detail

quiz.text: Which adds the most useful detail?
options: the fan with the cracked guard
quiz.explain: It identifies exactly which fan, which is what a phrase can do that one adjective cannot.
quiz.objective: Use adjective phrases to add detail

quiz.text: Moving a descriptive phrase can change what a sentence means.
quiz.explain: It attaches to whatever is nearest, so position carries meaning.
quiz.objective: Place a descriptive phrase next to what it describes

quiz.text: 'Families living below the dam' — the phrase describes…
quiz.objective: Use adjective phrases to add detail

quiz.text: In Chapter 18, how does Quixote describe Dulcinea?
options: As a lady of great beauty and noble birth
quiz.explain: Everyone else sees a farm girl. His description is the whole joke.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 8 English. Descriptive phrases are introduced by what they buy you — precision an adjective cannot reach — rather than by definition, and the bench example makes that concrete: on a table of parts, a phrase is how you specify which screw. Placement is the examinable half, and misplaced modifiers are taught through the read-it-literally test, which is both the diagnostic and the joke. The Dulcinea card closes the lesson neatly, since the novel's central character is built entirely out of one man's descriptive phrases.
discussion: What can a phrase do that a single adjective cannot?
How do you spot a misplaced modifier?
extension: Describe three objects on a table so precisely that nobody could pick the wrong one.
Find a misplaced modifier in something you wrote.
misconceptions: Putting the phrase far from its noun.
Thinking a phrase needs a verb.
Not reading the sentence literally to check.
